The methodological contribution is significant: matrix completion requires weaker assumptions than standard gravity-model estimators and handles multidimensional counterfactuals that conventional approaches cannot.
data.key_takeaway: Causal machine learning reveals that trade agreements create simultaneous winners and losers at the product level that aggregate statistics conceal—a warning against relying on average treatment effects for policy design.

Unlike existing single-turn benchmarks, MANTA's 1,088 five-turn dialogues expose two distinct failure modes: models that recognize welfare concerns in isolation but abandon them when pressed (value instability), and models that fail to surface welfare stakes proactively in everyday queries (low moral sensitivity). data.key_takeaway: An LLM that passes a standard safety check on ethical reasoning may still capitulate when users push back across multiple conversational turns — a gap that benchmark designers and deploying organizations need to account for.

data.centre_angle: This benchmark study demonstrates that welfare-relevant reasoning elicited in standard text prompts does not reliably transfer to agentic settings where models must take real actions with tools. Crucially, adding a single welfare-aware sentence to the system prompt produces dramatic gains in some models (47–63 percentage points for Claude and GPT-5.5) but minimal gains in others (under 12 points for DeepSeek and Gemini). data.centre_angle: This study demonstrates that perceived AI deception—distinct from designed deception intensity—exerts a consistent, negative causal effect on user evaluations in a high-engagement digital environment. From CAMO's perspective on the algorithmic and data foundations of trustworthy AI systems, the finding sharpens a measurement problem that matters well beyond gaming: designers and deployers may believe they have calibrated an AI behavior at an acceptable intensity, while users are perceiving something altogether different. The gap between intended system design and user attribution is precisely the kind of confound that rigorous causal identification—of the type explored in CAMO's work on algorithmic decision-making and endogenous data—needs to account for before drawing policy or product conclusions.
data.claude_summary: When players in Baldur's Gate 3 notice that AI-driven game mechanics are designed to deceive them, their satisfaction ratings fall—regardless of how intense that deception actually is. Using six years of Steam reviews and 54 version updates as a quasi-natural experiment, this study separates designer-intended deception intensity from players' perceived deception awareness. The key finding: any degree of deception awareness produces a monotonic negative effect on positive review rates, falsifying the common assumption that moderate perceived deception is tolerable or even enjoyable. High-intensity deception updates appear positive only because they coincide with new content releases—not because players appreciate the deception itself. Player experience does not reliably moderate these effects.
data.key_takeaway: Users who detect AI deception penalize it uniformly—there is no safe level of perceived deception that leaves satisfaction intact.

data.centre_angle: This study argues that LLMs, when used as synthetic participants in behavioural games, recover surface-level choice distributions but not the underlying reasoning process — they retrieve a strategic level rather than computing one. From CAMO's perspective on algorithmic foundations for trustworthy AI-driven decisions, this is a calibration problem with practical consequence: any organisation or researcher using LLM-simulated agents to pilot-test incentive schemes, mechanism designs, or market experiments should treat the outputs as category-level approximations, not behavioural ground truth. The gap between simulated cooperation and real end-game defection, for instance, would systematically mislead predictions about how employees or counterparties behave when stakes and horizons become concrete.
data.claude_summary: When LLMs are used as stand-ins for human participants in behavioural economics experiments, do they actually replicate human decision-making? This study tests that assumption across two classic games — a p-beauty contest and a public goods game — varying model scale, temperature, quantisation, and instruction-tuning across 360 conditions. The finding is that LLMs behave as fixed, scale-determined 'level-k' reasoners: larger models reason more steps ahead, but none update beliefs dynamically across rounds or backward-induct from a game's end. Human contributions to public goods decay over rounds; LLMs stay flat or rise. LLMs respond to horizon framing (indefinite vs finite) but ignore their actual position within that horizon, so no end-game defection appears. The implication is that LLMs simulate a cognitive category, not a cognitive process.
data.key_takeaway: LLMs mimic a fixed level of strategic reasoning set by model scale but do not update beliefs or backward-induct, making them unreliable substitutes for human participants in dynamic behavioural experiments.
